# High-Level Languages {#chapter-11-high-level-languages}

In this chapter we will begin to look at our first \"real-world\"
programming language. Assembly language is the language used at the
machine\'s level, but most people find coding in assembly language too
cumbersome for everyday use. Many computer languages have been invented
to make the programming task easier. Knowing a wide variety of languages
is useful for many reasons, including:

-   Different languages are based on different concepts, which will help
    you to learn different and better programming methods and ideas.

-   Different languages are good for different types of projects.

-   Different companies have different standard languages, so knowing
    more languages makes your skills more marketable.

-   The more languages you know, the easier it is to pick up new ones.

As a programmer, you will often have to pick up new languages.
Professional programmers can usually pick up a new language with about a
weeks worth of study and practice. Languages are simply tools, and
learning to use a new tool should not be something a programmer flinches
at. In fact, if you do computer consulting you will often have to learn
new languages on the spot in order to keep yourself employed. It will
often be your customer, not you, who decides what language is used. This
chapter will introduce you to a few of the languages available to you. I
encourage you to explore as many languages as you are interested in. I
personally try to learn a new language every few months.

Compiled and Interpreted Languages {#compiled-and-interpreted-languages}
----------------------------------

Many languages are *compiled* languages. When you write assembly
language, each instruction you write is translated into
exactly one machine instruction for processing. With compilers,
a statement can translate into one or hundreds of machine instructions.
In fact, depending on how advanced your compiler is, it might even
restructure parts of your code to make it faster. In assembly language
what you write is what you get.

There are also languages that are *interpreted* languages. These
languages require that the user run a program called an
*interpreter* that in turn runs the given program. These are
usually slower than compiled programs, since the interpreter has to read
and interpret the code as it goes along. However, in well-made
interpreters, this time can be fairly negligible. There is also a class
of hybrid languages which partially compile a program before execution
into byte-codes. This is done because the interpreter can read the
byte-codes much faster than it can read the regular language.

There are many reasons to choose one or the other. Compiled programs are
nice, because you don\'t have to already have an interpreter installed
in the user\'s machine. You have to have a compiler for the language,
but the users of your program don\'t. In an interpreted language, you
have to be sure that the user has an interpreter installed for your
program, and that the computer knows which interpreter to run your
program with. However, interpreted languages tend to be more flexible,
while compiled languages are more rigid.

Language choice is usually driven by available tools and support for
programming methods rather than by whether a language is compiled or
interpreted. In fact many languages have options for either one.

High-level languages, whether compiled or interpreted, are oriented
around you, the programmer, instead of around the machine. This opens
them up to a wide variety of features, which can include the following:

-   Being able to group multiple operations into a single expression.

-   Being able to use \"big values\" - values that are much more
    conceptual than the 8-byte numbers that computers normally deal with
    (for example, being able to view text strings as a single value
    rather than as a string of bytes).

-   Having access to better flow control constructs than
    just jumps.

-   Having a compiler to check types of value assignments and other
    assertions.

-   Having memory handled automatically, without the errors of handling
    it by hand (using memory after it was freed, or forgetting to free
    it).

-   Being able to work in a language that resembles the problem domain
    rather than the computer hardware.

So why does one choose one language over another? For example, many
choose Python because it has a clean syntax that often lends itself to
straightforward solutions, and a vast library of packages for just
about every protocol, type of data or science on the planet. Rust gives
the speed and control of a compiled language with a compiler that
catches memory errors before the program runs. JavaScript runs in every
web browser. Common LISP has more power and features than any other
environment for those willing to learn it. Scheme is the model of
simplicity and power combined together. C is the language in which most
operating systems are written, and its calling convention is the one
that all the others use to talk to each other.

Each language is different, and the more languages you know the better
programmer you will be. Knowing the concepts of different languages will
help you in all programming, because you can match the programming
language to the problem better, and you have a larger set of tools to
work with. Even if certain features aren\'t directly supported in the
language you are using, often they can be simulated. However, if you
don\'t have a broad experience with languages, you won\'t know of all
the possibilities you have to choose from.

Your First Rust Program {#your-first-rust-program}
-----------------------

Rust is a compiled language, like C, which it was designed to replace
in many places: it produces fast machine code, it doesn\'t need an
interpreter, and it can call (and be called from) code that follows the
system calling convention, as we saw in
[Chapter 8](08-sharing-functions-with-code-libraries.qmd#calling-assembly-from-rust-and-python).
Unlike C, its compiler checks that the program never uses memory that
was freed, never reads past the end of an array, and never lets two
threads change the same data at the same time. Here is your first Rust
program, which prints \"Hello World!\" to the screen and exits. Type it
in, and give it the name `011-01-hello-world.rs`:

```{.rust .numberLines include=resource/asm/011-01-hello-world.rs}
```

As you can see, it\'s a pretty simple program. To compile it, run the
command:

```{.bash}
rustc --edition 2024 -o 011-01-hello-world 011-01-hello-world.rs
```

To run the program, do:

```{.bash}
./011-01-hello-world
```

Let\'s look at how this program was put together.

Comments in Rust start with `//` and go to the end of the line, like
the `#` comments of our assembly language programs.

Then there is the line `fn main()`. This is the start of a function.
Rust functions are declared with `fn`, their name, their parameters in
parentheses and, after an arrow (`->`), the type of the value they
return. This one is called `main`, it has no parameters, and it returns
nothing. The body of the function is between the braces. You don\'t
have to worry about which registers hold the parameters, or about the
stack frame and its alignment - the compiler takes care of that for
you.

The `main` function is a special function in Rust - it is the start of
all Rust programs (much like `_start` in our assembly-language
programs). In fact, the program has a `_start` too: the compiler adds
one, from the C library, which prepares the program and then calls
Rust\'s own start-up code, which finally calls `main`. When `main`
returns, the program exits with status 0. The command-line arguments
are not parameters of `main`; the program asks for them with
`std::env::args()`, which gets them from the start-up code, which found
them on the stack, where Linux left them.

The next line prints the text. `println!` is a *macro*, not a function
(that is what the `!` means): the compiler expands it into code that
formats the text, adds a newline and calls the functions that write it
to STDOUT. In assembly language, you had to put the address of the text
and its length in registers, and then make the `write` system call.
Rust takes care of this complexity for you. We just have to type in the
string in quotations, and the compiler takes care of defining storage
for it, and of passing its address and its length. As you can see,
it\'s a lot less work.

As you can see, using high-level languages makes life much easier. It
also allows our programs to run on multiple platforms more easily. In
assembly language, your program is tied to both the operating system
and the hardware platform, while in compiled and interpreted languages
the same code can usually run on multiple operating systems and
hardware platforms. For example, this program can be built and executed
on x86-64 hardware running Linux®, Windows®, macOS® or most other
operating systems. In addition, it can also run on ARM processors, such
as the ones of phones, of the Raspberry Pi and of recent Apple
computers, without any change.

What the Compiler Generates {#what-the-compiler-generates}
---------------------------

A compiler translates your program into assembly language, or directly
into machine code, so we can compare its work with ours. Here is the
maximum program of
[Chapter 3](03-your-first-programs.qmd#finding-a-maximum-value) in Rust,
`011-02-maximum.rs`. Like `003-02-maximum`, it returns the largest
number of the list as its exit status code, 222:

```{.rust .numberLines include=resource/asm/011-02-maximum.rs}
```

`&[i64]` is a *slice*: the address of the first number and the number
of items, which Rust keeps together. `items[0]` is the first one, and
`&items[1..]` all the others. `rustc` can stop before making the
program and save the assembly language it generates, with
`--emit asm`. `-C opt-level=2` asks it to optimize, as it does for the
programs that people actually use:

```{.bash}
rustc --edition 2024 -C opt-level=2 --emit asm 011-02-maximum.rs
```

It writes `011-02-maximum.s`, in the same AT&T syntax that we use. This
is the beginning of the function `maximum`, generated by Rust 1.100.0
(we removed the lines that start with `.cfi`, which describe the stack
frame for debuggers):

```{.gnuassembler}
maximum:
	pushq	%rax
	testq	%rsi, %rsi
	je	.LBB5_25
	movq	(%rdi), %rax
	cmpq	$1, %rsi
	je	.LBB5_24
	leaq	(,%rsi,8), %rdx
	leaq	8(%rdi), %rcx
	addq	$-16, %rdx
	movl	%edx, %r8d
	shrl	$3, %r8d
	incl	%r8d
	andl	$7, %r8d
	je	.LBB5_5
	shll	$3, %r8d
	.p2align	4
.LBB5_4:
	movq	(%rcx), %r9
	cmpq	%rax, %r9
	cmovgq	%r9, %rax
	addq	$8, %rcx
	addq	$-8, %r8
	jne	.LBB5_4
```

There is a lot to recognize here:

-   The slice arrives as two parameters, as the calling convention
    says: the address in _%rdi_ and the number of items in _%rsi_. The
    result goes in _%rax_.

-   `testq %rsi, %rsi` checks if there are no items at all. In that
    case, `items[0]` doesn\'t exist, and the code at `.LBB5_25` (not
    shown) stops the program with an error message, a *panic*. Our
    assembly version would have read whatever was in memory. This is
    the safety that Rust adds, and it costs two instructions.

-   There is no `%rbp` frame. The compiler knows exactly where everything
    is relative to _%rsp_, so it doesn\'t need one (see the note on the
    frame pointer in
    [Chapter 12](12-optimization.qmd#the-frame-pointer)). The only
    `pushq` is `pushq %rax`, which saves nothing useful: it moves
    _%rsp_ by 8 so that it is a multiple of 16, in case the function
    calls the code that panics.

-   The loop at `.LBB5_4` is our loop, with a new instruction:
    `cmovgq %r9, %rax`, *conditional move if greater*, which copies
    _%r9_ to _%rax_ only if the last comparison said greater. It
    replaces the jump around a `movq`. Jumps that the processor can\'t
    predict are slow, and a conditional move never jumps.

-   The rest of the function (not shown, 46 more instructions) is the
    same loop *unrolled*: it handles eight items per iteration,
    one after the other, so the loop runs its counter and its jump
    eight times less often. The loop at `.LBB5_4` only handles the
    items that are left over.

Without `-C opt-level=2`, the function has 46 instructions too, but
very different ones: it keeps every variable in memory, on the stack,
much like our programs keep local variables, and it calls a separate
function to make the slice `&items[1..]` and another one for each step
of the loop. The optimizer turned the variables into registers and
*inlined* those functions: it copied their code into `maximum`, and
then simplified it. Compiler
writers know the processor very well, so reading the output of the
compiler is a good way to learn tricks like `cmovg`. The site
[Compiler Explorer][11-Godbolt] shows it as you type, for many
languages and compilers.

Python {#python}
------

Python is an interpreted language. Here is the same \"Hello World!\"
program in Python, `011-01-hello-world.py`:

```{.python .numberLines include=resource/asm/011-01-hello-world.py}
```

Since Python is interpreted, you don\'t need to compile or link it. Just
run it with the following command:

```{.bash}
python3 011-01-hello-world.py
```

As you can see, the Python version is even shorter than the Rust
version. With Python you don\'t have to declare any functions or
program entry points. You can just start typing commands and the
interpreter will run them as it comes to them. In fact this program only
has two lines of code, one of which is optional.

The first, optional line is used for UNIX machines to tell which
interpreter to use to run the program. The `#!` tells the computer that
this is an interpreted program, and `/usr/bin/env python3` tells the
computer to find the program `python3` and use it to interpret the
program. If you make the file executable (`chmod +x
011-01-hello-world.py`), you can run it as `./011-01-hello-world.py`.
However, since we ran the program by typing in `python3
011-01-hello-world.py`, we had already specified that we were using the
Python interpreter.

The next line calls a Python builtin function, `print`. This has one
parameter, the string to print. The program doesn\'t have an explicit
exit - it knows to exit simply because it runs off the end of the file.
It also knows to exit with status 0 because there were no errors while
it ran. You can see that interpreted languages are often focused on
letting you get working code as quickly as possible, without having to
do a lot of extra legwork.

One thing about Python that isn\'t so evident from this example is that
Python treats strings as a single value. In assembly language, we had
to program according to the computer\'s memory architecture, which
meant that strings had to be treated as a sequence of multiple values,
with a pointer to the first letter. Python pretends that strings can be
stored directly as values, and thus hides the complication of
manipulating them for you. Its numbers are values too, and they never
overflow: Python makes them as big as they need to be, at the cost of
speed.

Python doesn\'t run your program directly. It first compiles it into
*bytecode*, the instructions of a machine that doesn\'t exist, and then
runs the bytecode with its interpreter (this is the hybrid approach we
mentioned at the beginning of the chapter). Here is the maximum
program in Python, `011-02-maximum.py`:

```{.python .numberLines include=resource/asm/011-02-maximum.py}
```

The module `dis` shows the bytecode:

```{.bash}
python3 -m dis 011-02-maximum.py
```

This is the part for the function `maximum`, with Python 3.12 (the
numbers on the left are the lines of the program):

```
 16           2 LOAD_FAST                0 (items)
              4 LOAD_CONST               1 (0)
              6 BINARY_SUBSCR
             10 STORE_FAST               1 (largest)

 17          12 LOAD_FAST                0 (items)
             14 LOAD_CONST               2 (1)
             16 LOAD_CONST               0 (None)
             18 BINARY_SLICE
             20 GET_ITER
        >>   22 FOR_ITER                10 (to 46)
             26 STORE_FAST               2 (item)

 18          28 LOAD_FAST                2 (item)
             30 LOAD_FAST                1 (largest)
             32 COMPARE_OP              68 (>)
             36 POP_JUMP_IF_TRUE         1 (to 40)
             38 JUMP_BACKWARD            9 (to 22)

 19     >>   40 LOAD_FAST                2 (item)
             42 STORE_FAST               1 (largest)
             44 JUMP_BACKWARD           12 (to 22)

 17     >>   46 END_FOR

 20          48 LOAD_FAST                1 (largest)
             50 RETURN_VALUE
```

It looks like assembly language, and it is: the assembly language of
the Python interpreter. The bytecode machine has no registers, only a
stack: `LOAD_FAST` pushes a variable, `COMPARE_OP` pops two values and
pushes the result, and `POP_JUMP_IF_TRUE` is a conditional jump. But
each of these instructions is a small program for the interpreter. For
example, `COMPARE_OP` has to find out the types of the two values (they
could be numbers, strings or anything else), and choose how to compare
them. The machine code of the Rust version compares two registers with
one instruction, `cmpq`. That is the main reason why interpreted
programs are slower, and also why they are so flexible: the same
`maximum` works for a list of numbers or a list of strings.

There are many other languages. Perl, for example, is an interpreted
language like Python that is very good at processing text, and C is the
compiled language in which Linux and most of its libraries are written.
Learn as many as you can.

Review {#review-9}
------

### Know the Concepts {#know-the-concepts-9}

-   What is the difference between an interpreted language and a
    compiled language?

-   What is bytecode?

-   What reasons might cause you to need to learn a new programming
    language?

### Use the Concepts {#use-the-concepts-9}

-   Learn the basic syntax of a new programming language. Re-code one of
    the programs in this book in that language.

-   In the program you wrote in the question above, what specific things
    were automated in the programming language you chose?

-   Modify your program so that it runs 10,000 times in a row, both in
    assembly language and in your new language. Then run the `time`
    command to see which is faster. Which does come out ahead? Why do
    you think that is?

-   Use `rustc --emit asm` (or Compiler Explorer) to see the assembly
    language of a small Rust function of your own, with and without
    `-C opt-level=2`. Which instructions do you recognize?

-   How does the programming language\'s input/output methods differ
    from that of the Linux system calls?

### Going Further {#going-further-9}

-   Having seen languages which have such brevity as Python, why do you
    think this book started you with a language as verbose as assembly
    language?

-   How do you think high level languages have affected the process of
    programming?

-   Why do you think so many languages exist?

-   Learn two new high level languages. How do they differ from each
    other? How are they similar? What approach to problem-solving does
    each take?
